A political leader of the Métis, a people of mixed First Nations and French or Scottish descent on the Canadian prairies, and a founder of the province of Manitoba. He led two resistance movements against the government of Canada and was hanged for treason.

In 1869 the Hudson's Bay Company sold its huge territory, Rupert's Land, to the new Canadian government without asking the people living there. At the Red River settlement, Riel, then 25, set up a provisional government. Its execution of a Canadian prisoner, Thomas Scott, enraged English Canada. But the talks it forced led to the Manitoba Act of 1870, which created the province with guarantees of land and of French and Catholic rights. Riel had to flee into exile in the United States.

In 1885 the Métis of the Saskatchewan valley called him back. Their North-West Rebellion was crushed by troops brought by the new Canadian Pacific Railway. Riel was tried and hanged at Regina. French Canadians saw him as a martyr; English Ontario as a traitor. Today he is honoured as a founder of Manitoba.
